title: Your vow
hook: a vow in your own words for the years ahead
tomorrow: a man with a terrible past must say one true sentence. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, refuge again: the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and an island inside you too. Three jewels. Now, where you'll stand.

A coach says you've made the team; a manager offers the promotion. The win is right there. The young seeker in the Majjhima Nikaya turned one down, twice. He studies with Alara Kalama and reaches the same meditation his teacher reached. Alara offers to lead the community with him, as equals. He says no and walks away. Then he studies with Uddaka Ramaputta, reaches that height too, and is offered the place of teacher. He walks away again. What wasn't enough? The sutta says it plainly: those states didn't lead to awakening, to peace, to the end of suffering.
screen: `THE WIN IS RIGHT THERE.` → `ALARA: LEAD WITH ME.` → `UDDAKA: BE THE TEACHER.` → `HE WALKS AWAY. TWICE.`

segments.voice: In another sutta, the Buddha names two things he learned along the way: not to settle for good states, and not to shrink back while striving. Then he gives the resolve he made, and he says it in the body. Let only skin and sinew and bone remain, let the flesh and blood dry up; I will not stop until I reach what human strength can reach. That's a vow you can feel: the skin of your hands, the cords at your wrists, the bones you're sitting on right now. Buddhists have a word for this: adhitthana, resolve, a vow set down like a foundation stone. Theravada lists it among the perfections, the qualities a Buddha-to-be grows over lifetimes. In Zen halls, the bodhisattva vows are chanted after sitting: beings are numberless, I vow to free them. The words differ from school to school. The shape is the same. A vow isn't a wish. It's where you stand when the good-enough offer arrives. Year five is near its summit, and this block asks for one thing: a vow in your own words, for the years ahead. Not the Buddha's words. Yours. Small enough to keep, and set down by hand, like a stone.
screen: `DON'T SETTLE FOR GOOD.` · `SKIN, SINEW AND BONE.` · `ADHITTHANA: A FOUNDATION STONE.` · `IN YOUR OWN WORDS, BY HAND.` · then, large: `MY VOW.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and paper, and feel the pen's weight and the paper under the side of your hand. Write one sentence that begins I vow, for the years ahead, small enough to keep. Then put the pen down, rest both hands flat on the page, and feel the bones of your hands while the sit runs.
Your vow: adhitthana, resolve, the foundation stone you stand on when good enough comes calling.
Keep this: my vow, in my own words, by my own hand. Forty-three days into the block.

screen: `DAY 1768 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 43 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: ONE TRUE SENTENCE FROM A MAN WITH A PAST. WHICH?`

howItsDone: Buddhists make resolves at many scales: Theravada practitioners speak of adhitthana as a perfection, and in Zen and other Mahayana communities the bodhisattva vows are chanted together, often at the end of a sitting.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta: leaving Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta)
Anguttara Nikaya 2.5 (not settling for wholesome states; the skin, sinew and bone resolve)
The four great bodhisattva vows (chanted in Zen communities, traced to Zhiyi)

notes: MN 26 paraphrased: Alara Kalama attains the base of nothingness and offers to lead the community jointly; Uddaka Ramaputta (whose father Rama attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) offers him the place of teacher. Both times he leaves because the Dhamma 'does not lead to disenchantment... to nibbana'. Confirm 'reaches that height too' is fair for Uddaka (the sutta says he realized what Rama had realized).

AN 2.5 paraphrased: the two things are discontent with wholesome states and not shrinking back in striving; the resolve 'willingly let only skin, sinews and bones remain...' is the Buddha's own. Confirm wording.
Adhitthana as one of the perfections (Buddhavamsa list); 'over lifetimes' reflects the Theravada bodhisatta path. Confirm.
'Beings are numberless, I vow to free them' is a paraphrase of the first of the four great vows chanted in Zen, not a quotation and not a new prayer. Confirm.
Practice: write by hand (rotation). Mai's arc: Ông kept a vow from his youth in his wallet and asks Mai to write hers.
Surprising fact: the Buddha phrased his own resolve in skin, sinew and bone (AN 2.5).
